I've found that if there is a physiological reason behind bad behavior (lack of sleep, poor diet, discomfort due to illness) punishment will exacerbate the problem. The trick is knowing your child and identifying when they're uncomfortable and when they're just being an ass.

While this is true, and understanding your kid > blindly punishing them, you also don't want to misinterpret in the other direction either.

Think of how infuriating it was as a kid to have a legitimate emotional problem and have it dismissed with "wow....somebody sounds tired... yea I think it's time for a nap". Or, someone in junior high/high school age to have their feelings dismissed because they were out partying all night and haven't been getting enough sleep lately. The root cause here is still some problem the kid is having with something that is bothering them, and you're absolutely right in saying that noticing that there is an external cause of them acting out is key, but don't assume you know what that is or how to fix it... you're going to have to talk to them, and they aren't going to tell you strait away.

If he has nothing left to lose and is miserable, better believe he is going to make sure you are miserable too. I was the same way as a kid.

If he isn't harming himself or bothering others, pretty much let him do what he wants. As for consequences, make it fit what he's doing. Don't want to wear sunscreen and a cap? Then you can play inside instead instead of going to the park. Not going to take a bath? Then he can't go out to play or have friends over, and he has to eat in his room where he won't be able to choose what he eats from the table. Don't want to help clean the toys up? Then clean them and put them away for the rest of the day, and if it continues to be an issue then he has to only play in a small room or cornered off area (like a 4 foot space between the sofa and wall) instead of being free to play around the house until he can show he is able to handle putting his toys away for a predetermined amount of time. Use stickers or a stamp to show progress, and then after a week or whatever of cleaning, he "wins" the ability to play in the living room. I'd say for a 5 year old a 1 day long punishment, like not being able to watch TV because they continue to turn it up really loud, is pretty harsh and should only be used for repeat misdeeds.

But for a 5 year old, it's pretty easy to give them choices that still get you to the point you want. Like "Do you want to wear the red cap or the purple cap?" or "Do you want a bath with or without bubbles?" or making cleaning up into a game where you throw the toys into the bins like a game of basketball. It it's something he doesn't like to do, like brushing his teeth, take him to the store and let him choose the toothbrush and toothpaste he wants - and don't be afraid to tell him "X brand is too expensive. You can choose between 1, 2, 3 and 4"

TL;DR - Give the illusion of choice and give logical consequences

When I started to move away from Windows, at the turn of the century, my first step was actually to start looking for cross-platform, possibly open source, alternatives to all of the programs I was using, and switch to them one by one. It wasn't always easy, since especially at the time the gap in usability (when not quality altogether) between FLOSS and proprietary software was much larger than now, except when it came to software development tools and “satellite” software, but it was an investment that paid off in a few years, in terms of both money and sanity.

It takes time and effort, because even when the alternatives are good (or better) than the leading Windows programs, they often have a different approach to the UI (not necessarily inferior, but different enough to put off people that are used to doing things “a certain way”). But IMO it's fully worth it.

(And if you still end up needing that one specific Windows-only program, WINE or virtual machines come in handy.)
How well does WINE work? Isn't it resource intensive to run like an emulator?

WINE is not particularly resource intensive. Aside from allowing the loading and execution of Windows executable, for most intents and purposes, it works pretty much like most native toolkits do, mapping the Win32 APIs to lower-level native APIs (for example, consider the UI drawing stuff: most native software does not use Xlib directly, but rather something like GTK+ or Qt, and going through Win32 rather than GTK+ or Qt isn't more expensive). Things get more complicated for some APIs such as DirectX/Direct3D which have to be remapped to, say, OpenGL, which might not be as straightforward as for most other things. There you might get some performance penalty, so that for example when using WINE for games it's often better to use the OpenGL renderer of the game rather than Direct3D.
